questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of interpolation search?

answer.text: Estimate the probe position from the target's value relative to the range endpoints, like looking up a name in a phone book

feedback.text: Correct — it interpolates where the target likely lies rather than always probing the middle.

answer.text: Always compare the exact middle element to halve the interval

feedback.text: That is binary search; interpolation search predicts a position from the value.

answer.text: Scan every element in order from the start

feedback.text: That is linear search.

answer.text: Split the range using Fibonacci numbers

feedback.text: That is Fibonacci search.

generalfeedback.text: Interpolation search computes a probe index by interpolating the target value between the low and high key values — a dictionary/phone-book style lookup.

questiontext.text: On sorted, uniformly distributed numeric data, what is the average-case time complexity of interpolation search?

feedback.text: Correct — on uniform data the estimate is very accurate, giving O(log log n).
That is binary search; interpolation does better on uniform data.
That is the worst case on skewed data, not the uniform-data average.
Too optimistic; the average is O(log log n).

generalfeedback.text: When keys are uniformly distributed the value-based estimate lands very close to the target, giving an average of O(log log n).

questiontext.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of interpolation search on skewed / non-uniform data?

feedback.text: Correct — a badly skewed distribution makes each estimate poor, degrading to a linear scan.
That is only the average on uniformly distributed data.
No — unlike binary search, interpolation can degrade to O(n) on skewed data.
Far too optimistic for the worst case.

generalfeedback.text: If the data is highly non-uniform the interpolated probe is repeatedly off, so the worst case is O(n).

questiontext.text: Under which conditions does interpolation search perform best?

answer.text: The data is sorted and its values are roughly uniformly distributed

feedback.text: Correct — sorting is required, and uniform values make the estimate accurate.

answer.text: The data is unsorted but uniformly distributed

feedback.text: No — like binary search it still requires sorted input.

answer.text: The data is sorted but heavily skewed

feedback.text: Skew hurts it — that is the O(n) worst case.
No — it requires sorted input to interpolate a position.

generalfeedback.text: Interpolation search requires sorted input and shines when values are uniformly distributed; skew degrades it toward O(n).

questiontext.text: Which statements about interpolation search are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It requires the input to be sorted

feedback.text: Yes — it interpolates a position within an ordered range.

answer.text: Its average is O(log log n) on uniform data but its worst case is O(n) on skewed data

feedback.text: Yes — performance depends heavily on the distribution.

answer.text: It works correctly on unsorted arrays

feedback.text: No — it requires sorted input.

answer.text: It guarantees O(log n) even on highly skewed data

feedback.text: No — on skewed data it can degrade to O(n).

generalfeedback.text: Interpolation search: sorted input, value-based probing, O(log log n) average on uniform data, O(n) worst case, O(1) space.

questiontext.text: Interpolation search requires the input array to be sorted.

feedback.text: Correct — it interpolates a probe position within an ordered range.
No — sorted input is required.

name.text: Interpolation vs binary on skewed data

questiontext.text: Interpolation search is always faster than binary search, even on highly skewed data.

feedback.text: No — on skewed / non-uniform data it can degrade to O(n), worse than binary search's O(log n).
Correct — its advantage holds only on uniformly distributed data.

questiontext.text: This search estimates the probe position by linear ______ of the target value between the range endpoints. Give the one-word term.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
